prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

These items come from talks, interviews, threads, comments and advice, not only from papers. Some are advice the speaker gives or a view he argues for, not a decision his own team made. Write each of those as a decision point a research team faces ("A research team ..."), so that the advice or view is one possible resolution of it; the rules above apply unchanged. The text before the decision may be a transcript or a comment thread: use it only for the situation.

=== key 63d8f3048c15

Problem: Whether human-machine integration / brain-augmented cognition is a promising line to expect progress from
Write-up text before the decision: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/qRtD4WqKRYEtT5pi3/the-next-decades-might-be-wild?commentId=ZYRghTzkCeiZHXmt3 PARENT (not his words): This scenario certainly seems plausible, if overly benign and slow. === key a9e2d83fe922
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: How fast AI capabilities shown in the lab translate into economic transformation and self-improvement
Write-up text before the decision: AI. You have what appear to be APS-AIs first showing up in the 2030s. Why not the 20s? Is it because they need to have more parameters, training time, etc. than is feasible in the 30s? Because e.g. they need to be 100T+ parameters trained compute-optimally where each data point is a many-step trajectory? 2\. You speak of research being increasingly automated, e.g. coding productivity doubling, language-model-powered search being much better... Why hasn't this accelerated progress towards AGI / APS-AI? I'd argue that progress will start noticeably accelerating in the twenties. 3\. Why is there no singularity in this story? It looks like your story has APS-AI appearing in the thirties, and also "Chatbots have long passed all kinds of Turing tests and start to fuck around on the internet." And of course they have automated most AI research and large parts of the economy. Why does it take 10-20 more years to get to superintelligence? HIS COMMENT: I think it's mostly my skepticism about extremely fast economic transformations. Like GPT-3 could probably automate more parts of the economy today but somehow it just takes a while for people to understand that and get it to work in practice. I also expect that it will take a couple of years between showing the capabilities of new AI systems in the lab and widespread economic impact just because humans take a while to adapt (at least with narrow systems). At some point (maybe in 2030) we will reach a level where AI is as capable as humans in many tasks and then the question is obviously how fast it can self-improve.

=== key 3842b6ff971e
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: Whether layer norm is the main reason tokens should be thought of as directions
Write-up text before the decision: sformer Token Vectors Are Not Points in Space" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/pHPmMGEMYefk9jLeh/llm-basics-embedding-spaces-transformer-token-vectors-are?commentId=ZpJRnGzR4B9spaZzk PARENT (not his words): I'm pretty sure the main reason it's good to think of features/tokens as being directions is because of layer norm. All any "active" component of the neural network "sees" is the direction of the residual stream, and not its magnitude, since layer norm's output is always norm 1 (before applying the scale and bias terms). You do mention this in part 1.2, but I think it should be mentioned elsewhere (e.g. Intro, Part 2, Conclusion), as it seems pretty important? HIS COMMENT: I agree that the layer norm does some work here but I think some parts of the explanation can be attributed to the inductive bias of the cross-entropy loss. [...] My intuition was roughly: \- the softmax doesn't care about absolute size, only about the relative differences of the logits. \- thus, the network merely has to make the correct logits really big and the incorrect logits small \- to get the logits, you take the inner product of the activations and the unembedding. The more aligned the directions of the correct class with the corresponding unembedding weights are (i.e. the smaller their cosine similarity), the bigger the logits. \- Thus, direction matters more than distance.
